days.title: Why Spark, Its Trade-offs, and the Driver, Executor and Cluster Manager Roles

concepts.heading: Advantages of Spark
concepts.body: Spark is a unified engine for large-scale data processing. One engine and one set of high-level APIs in Python, Scala, Java and R cover batch SQL, streaming, machine learning and graphs, so a team does not stitch several systems together. Its main speed advantage over disk-based MapReduce is that executors can keep a working dataset in memory between actions: a loop that reads the same data thirty times pays for the storage read once, then serves later passes from the cache. Spill to local disk keeps jobs running when data does not fit, so memory is an optimization rather than a requirement. Transformations are lazy, so the Catalyst optimizer sees the whole query and can rewrite it, push filters down to sources such as Parquet and pick join strategies before any work starts. Lost partitions are rebuilt from lineage, the recorded chain of transformations, which gives fault tolerance without replicating every intermediate result. The same code runs on a laptop in local mode or on Kubernetes, YARN or a standalone cluster.

concepts.heading: Challenges of Spark
concepts.body: Spark is powerful but not free of cost. The most common trouble is the shuffle: wide operations such as joins on large tables, groupBy and distinct move data across the network and write shuffle files to disk, so they dominate runtime. Data skew makes one partition far larger than the rest, so one task keeps a whole stage waiting. Memory needs tuning, because executors can fail with out-of-memory errors or spend too much time in garbage collection, and a collect on a large result can exhaust the driver (spark.driver.maxResultSize defaults to 1g and aborts the job above it). Very many small input files add per-file open cost (Spark models it with spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes) and scheduling overhead. PySpark runs Python UDFs in separate Python worker processes, so rows are serialized between the JVM and Python (pickled by default, or through Arrow when enabled), which is why built-in functions are usually preferred. Finally, a distributed program is harder to debug than a single process: errors surface in executor logs, and lazy evaluation means a bug may appear far from the line that caused it.

concepts.heading: Driver, Executors and the Cluster Manager
concepts.body: A Spark application is a driver program plus executors. The driver runs your main function and creates the SparkSession (and the SparkContext inside it). It builds the plan, splits work into jobs, stages and tasks, and schedules tasks on executors. Executors are processes launched on worker nodes that run tasks and keep cached data in memory or on disk; each application has its own executors, which stay up for the whole application and run tasks in several threads. The cluster manager is an external service that hands out resources: standalone, YARN or Kubernetes. Spark is agnostic to which one, as long as it can acquire executor processes. The driver must accept incoming connections from its executors for its whole lifetime, so it should be network addressable from the workers and run close to them. Because each application has separate executor JVMs, two applications cannot share data without writing it to external storage. The driver also serves the web UI, typically on port 4040.

concepts.heading: Cores, Memory and Task Slots
concepts.body: Resources are set per executor. spark.executor.cores is the number of cores per executor (the default is 1 on YARN and all available cores of the worker in standalone mode), and spark.executor.memory is the JVM heap (default 1g). Each task needs spark.task.cpus cores, default 1, so the tasks that run at once in an executor equal executor cores divided by task cpus, rounded down. Total parallelism is executors times that number: 4 executors with 5 cores and one cpu per task give 20 task slots. A stage with 100 tasks then runs in five waves. Executor memory is not all usable for data: spark.memory.fraction (default 0.6) of heap minus 300 MB is shared by execution and storage, and spark.memory.storageFraction (default 0.5) of that region is immune to eviction by execution. For PySpark and other off-heap use, spark.executor.memoryOverhead adds non-heap memory on YARN and Kubernetes, executor memory times 0.10 by default with a 384 MiB minimum. Driver memory is spark.driver.memory, also 1g by default, and in client mode it must be set through spark-submit rather than in code.

examPoints: The driver builds the plan and schedules tasks; executors run tasks and hold cached data; the cluster manager only allocates resources.
Task slots = executors x floor(executor cores / spark.task.cpus); a 100-task stage on 20 slots runs in 5 waves.
Shuffles, skew, tiny files and Python UDF serialization are the usual challenges; in-memory reuse and lazy optimization are the advantages.

quiz.q: A job on 6 executors, each with 4 cores and the default spark.task.cpus, has a stage of 120 tasks of equal length. How many waves of tasks does that stage need?
choices: 4 waves, because 24 slots are used four times for the first 96 tasks and the rest follow
5 waves, because each of the 24 slots runs five tasks in turn
6 waves, because there are 6 executors and each takes its share one after another
30 waves, because only one task runs on an executor at any moment
quiz.explain: Slots = 6 x floor(4 / 1) = 24, and 120 / 24 = 5 waves. Executors run tasks in several threads, so one task per executor is wrong, and the number of executors alone does not set the wave count.

quiz.q: Which process requests executors from YARN or Kubernetes, sends tasks to them and, in client mode, runs in the process that submitted the application?
choices: The executor, which asks the cluster manager for more peers when work arrives
The cluster manager, which also compiles the user code into a plan
The driver, which owns the SparkSession and schedules the tasks
The worker node, which assigns tasks to executors on a schedule
quiz.explain: The driver holds the SparkSession, builds the plan and schedules tasks; with the cluster manager it acquires executors. The cluster manager only allocates resources, and executors only run tasks and store data. Deploy mode decides whether the driver runs outside the cluster (client) or inside it (cluster).

days.recap: Spark wins through one engine, in-memory reuse, lazy optimization and lineage-based recovery, and loses time to shuffles, skew, tiny files, memory limits and Python serialization. The driver plans and schedules, the cluster manager hands out resources, and executors with cores and memory run the tasks.

days.title: DataFrame and Dataset, the SparkSession Lifecycle, Caching and the Job-Stage-Task Hierarchy

concepts.heading: DataFrame versus Dataset
concepts.body: A Dataset is a distributed collection with strong typing and lambda functions, built on Spark SQL's optimized engine. The Dataset API exists in Scala and Java only; Python has no Dataset API. A DataFrame is a Dataset organized into named columns, like a table. In Scala and Java it is a Dataset of Row objects, and in Python (and R) it is the only structured API you have. For a PySpark developer the practical answer is therefore always DataFrame. The main benefit of the typed Dataset is that a mistyped field fails at compile time in Scala or Java; a DataFrame checks column names and types when the query is analyzed, at runtime. SQL, DataFrame and Dataset code all use the same execution engine, so you can mix them in one program. The older RDD API sits below them, and Spark SQL's interfaces give Spark more information about the data and the computation than RDDs do, which is why DataFrames are preferred.

concepts.heading: The SparkSession Lifecycle
concepts.body: SparkSession is the entry point to DataFrame and SQL functionality. You build one with SparkSession.builder, optionally set appName and config values, and call getOrCreate(). That call returns the existing global default session if a valid one exists, otherwise it creates a new session and makes it the global default, so calling it twice does not start two engines. The pyspark shell already provides a session named spark. Builder options are used when a new session is created; runtime SQL settings can be changed afterwards with spark.conf.set. Deploy-level settings such as spark.driver.memory in client mode cannot be changed from code. newSession() returns a session with its own SQL configuration, temporary views and UDFs but the same SparkContext and table cache, which is how isolated sessions share a cluster. spark.stop() stops the underlying SparkContext; after that the application's executors are released and DataFrames from that session can no longer run jobs. Stop the session when the application is finished, not after each query.

concepts.heading: Caching, Storage Levels and Garbage Collection
concepts.body: Because transformations are lazy, a DataFrame used by several actions is recomputed from its source each time unless you persist it. df.cache() is shorthand for persist() with the default storage level, MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER for DataFrames (changed from memory-only in 3.0). The cache is lazy: nothing is stored until the first action materializes the partitions. Levels in PySpark include MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK, DISK_ONLY and replicated variants ending in _2. Spark evicts old partitions in least-recently-used order, and unpersist() releases the cache early. Cached partitions that no longer fit in memory are recomputed under MEMORY_ONLY, or written to disk under MEMORY_AND_DISK. Garbage collection cost grows with the number of Java objects, so large caches of deserialized objects can cause long GC pauses; the tuning guide suggests serialized caching or fewer objects to lower it. If old-generation memory fills up, lower spark.memory.fraction so less is cached. Since Spark 4.0 the default JDK is 17 with the G1 collector.

concepts.heading: Jobs, Stages and Tasks
concepts.body: The execution hierarchy has four levels. An application is the driver plus its executors. Each action, such as count, collect or a write, spawns a job. Spark divides each job into stages at shuffle boundaries: operations that need no data movement between partitions (select, filter, withColumn, map-style work) are narrow and are pipelined inside one stage, while a wide operation such as groupBy, a sort-merge join or repartition ends a stage because data must be redistributed. A stage is a set of tasks that depend on earlier stages. A task is the smallest unit of work: it processes one partition and is sent to one executor. A stage therefore has as many tasks as its input has partitions. So df.groupBy('k').count().collect() is one job, normally two stages (the scan with partial aggregation, then the final aggregation after the shuffle), and as many tasks per stage as partitions. The Jobs, Stages and Storage tabs of the web UI show exactly this tree. Two actions on the same DataFrame make two jobs.

examPoints: Python has no Dataset API: in PySpark a DataFrame is the structured API; Scala and Java DataFrames are Dataset[Row].
cache() uses MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER for DataFrames and is lazy; unpersist() frees it, otherwise eviction is least-recently-used.
One action = one job; a shuffle ends a stage; one task processes one partition.

quiz.q: A PySpark developer calls df.cache() and then df.count() and df.show(). Which statement describes what happens?
choices: cache() immediately reads all data into memory, so the later count needs no job
The first action fills the cache using MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER; later actions reuse it
Both actions recompute the data from the source because cache() has no effect without a StorageLevel
The cache is stored only on the driver so that show() can print it without executors
quiz.explain: cache() only marks the DataFrame; the first action computes and stores the partitions, and later actions reuse them. It does not need an explicit level, and partitions live on executors, not on the driver.

quiz.q: A job runs df.filter(...).groupBy('k').agg(...).write.parquet(path). How many jobs and how many stages does Spark normally create?
choices: 1 job and 2 stages, because the groupBy shuffle ends the first stage
2 jobs and 2 stages, because the filter and the aggregation each trigger a job
1 job and 1 stage, because only wide operations create new jobs
3 jobs and 3 stages, because the filter, the aggregation and the write are separate actions
quiz.explain: Only the write is an action, so there is one job; the groupBy shuffle splits it into a map-side stage and a final stage. Filter is a narrow transformation and starts no job.

days.recap: DataFrame is the structured API in PySpark; getOrCreate() returns the one default session and spark.stop() ends the SparkContext. Cache is lazy, defaults to MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER and is evicted least-recently-used. Each action is a job, shuffles split jobs into stages, and each task works on one partition.

days.title: Partitions and Shuffles, Lazy Evaluation, and the Spark Modules

concepts.heading: Partitions and Shuffles
concepts.body: A partition is a slice of a dataset that one task processes, so the partition count sets the parallelism. When Spark reads files it packs data into partitions of up to spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, 128 MB by default. A shuffle redistributes data across the cluster so that rows with the same key meet; it is triggered by groupBy, most joins, distinct, orderBy and repartition. The map side writes shuffle files to local disk and the reduce side fetches them over the network. The number of output partitions of a DataFrame shuffle is spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, default 200. Adaptive Query Execution (on by default since 3.2) can coalesce those shuffle partitions at runtime, so the final count may be lower than 200. repartition(n) always shuffles and can increase or decrease the count; coalesce(n) only merges existing partitions without a full shuffle, and if you request more than the current count it stays at the current count. The two differ in cost: coalesce is cheap but may leave uneven partitions.

concepts.heading: Transformations, Actions and Lazy Evaluation
concepts.body: Transformations create a new dataset from an existing one and are lazy: select, filter, withColumn, join, groupBy().agg() and orderBy only add a step to the plan. Actions force computation and return a result to the driver or write output: count, collect, show, take, first, and write operations such as df.write.parquet. This laziness lets Spark optimize the whole chain at once and avoid reading data that no action needs. Transformations are either narrow, where each output partition depends on one input partition (filter, select, map), or wide, where data crosses partitions through a shuffle (groupBy, join, distinct, repartition). Narrow steps are pipelined in a single stage. Since nothing runs until an action, errors in a bad column name show up at analysis time, but data-dependent errors show up only when an action runs. df.printSchema() and df.explain() are not actions: they read the plan, not the data. A DataFrame is also immutable; each transformation returns a new one and the original is unchanged.

concepts.heading: Reading Plans and Lineage
concepts.body: Spark records every DataFrame's lineage, the chain of transformations from the source. The driver turns your code into a logical plan, the Catalyst optimizer rewrites it into an optimized logical plan, and a physical plan is chosen. df.explain() prints the physical plan, and explain('formatted') or explain(True) shows more detail. An Exchange node in the plan marks a shuffle and therefore a stage boundary; a BroadcastExchange marks a broadcast. If a partition is lost because an executor died, Spark recomputes only that partition by replaying the lineage, which is the basis of its fault tolerance. Long lineages are expensive to replay, so iterative loops sometimes truncate them with checkpointing or caching. Reading explain output is a core developer skill: look for Exchange to count shuffles, for PushedFilters to confirm that filters reach the file source, and for the join type, for example BroadcastHashJoin or SortMergeJoin.

concepts.heading: The Spark Modules
concepts.body: Spark Core provides the engine: scheduling, memory management, fault recovery and the RDD API. Spark SQL, with DataFrames and Datasets, is the module for structured data and the one used in most new code. Structured Streaming builds on it to process unbounded data with the same DataFrame operations. MLlib is the machine learning library; its DataFrame-based API lives in pyspark.ml, while the older RDD-based pyspark.mllib is in maintenance mode. The pandas API on Spark lets pandas-style code scale out on a cluster (import pyspark.pandas). GraphX handles graph processing. Spark Connect is a client-server layer that lets thin clients send DataFrame plans to a remote Spark server. A choice question usually reads like this: structured batch query is Spark SQL, an unbounded stream is Structured Streaming, scalable model training is pyspark.ml, and an existing pandas workflow that must scale is the pandas API on Spark. DStream-based Spark Streaming is the old API; Structured Streaming replaced it for new work.

examPoints: repartition(n) shuffles and can raise or lower the count; coalesce(n) only merges partitions without a full shuffle and cannot increase it.
Actions (count, collect, show, write) run jobs; transformations are lazy, and narrow ones pipeline in one stage while wide ones add a shuffle.
Pick the module from the workload: Spark SQL for tables, Structured Streaming for streams, pyspark.ml for models, pandas API on Spark for pandas code.

quiz.q: A DataFrame has 8 partitions. What does df.coalesce(16) return?
choices: A DataFrame with 16 partitions created by a full shuffle
A DataFrame with 8 partitions, because coalesce cannot increase the count
An error, because coalesce only accepts a smaller number than the current count
A DataFrame with 16 partitions made by splitting each existing partition without moving data
quiz.explain: coalesce is a narrow merge, and requesting more partitions than exist leaves the count unchanged. repartition(16) is the call that shuffles to a larger number.

quiz.q: A script builds df2 = df.filter('x > 5').select('x', 'y').withColumn('z', col('x') + 1) and then calls df2.printSchema(). How much data does Spark process at that point?
choices: The whole dataset, because filter must run before the schema is known
Only the rows where x is greater than 5, because the filter is applied during schema printing
The sample used for schema inference only, which is read from the source files
No data, because the steps are transformations and printSchema reads the plan, not the rows
quiz.explain: All three steps are lazy transformations, and printSchema is not an action; it reads the analyzed plan. Data is processed only when an action such as count or write runs.

days.recap: Partitions are the unit of parallelism; shuffles create new stages and default to 200 partitions that AQE may coalesce. repartition shuffles, coalesce only merges. Transformations are lazy and actions run jobs, with explain showing Exchange nodes. Choose Spark SQL, Structured Streaming, pyspark.ml or the pandas API on Spark by workload.

days.title: Reading and Writing with JDBC and Files, SQL on Files and Save Modes

concepts.heading: Reading and Writing Files
concepts.body: spark.read returns a DataFrameReader and df.write a DataFrameWriter. The generic form is spark.read.format('csv').option(...).load(path), and shortcuts such as spark.read.parquet(path), .csv, .json and .orc do the same. The default format is Parquet (spark.sql.sources.default). Readers accept a directory or a glob, so one call can read many files. File sources have defaults worth knowing. CSV reads header=false and inferSchema=false, so every column is a string named _c0, _c1 and so on unless you set header and inferSchema (inference costs an extra pass) or pass a schema. CSV mode is PERMISSIVE by default for corrupt records. JSON expects JSON Lines: each line is one self-contained object, and a regular multi-line JSON file needs option('multiLine', True). All built-in file sources discover partition columns from directory names like country=US and add them as columns. Writes create a directory of part files, one per partition, not a single file; to write one file, reduce to one partition first, accepting the lost parallelism. partitionBy('col') writes a directory per distinct value.

concepts.heading: Reading and Writing with JDBC
concepts.body: The JDBC source reads from and writes to relational databases. You put the driver jar on the classpath and give the url, a table in dbtable or a query in query, and credentials. dbtable accepts anything valid in a FROM clause, so a parenthesized subquery with an alias works; dbtable and query cannot be used together, and query cannot be combined with partitionColumn. By default a JDBC read uses one partition and one connection, so it does not scale. To parallelize, set partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions together; the column must be numeric, date or timestamp. The bounds only decide the stride and do not filter rows, so all rows of the table are still returned. numPartitions also caps concurrent connections, and a write with more partitions than that is coalesced down to the limit. fetchsize (default 0, which leaves the driver's own default in place) sets rows per round trip on reads, and batchsize (default 1000) sets rows per insert batch on writes. Pushdown of filters, aggregates and limits is on by default, so the database does part of the work.

concepts.heading: SQL Directly on Files
concepts.body: You can query a file without loading it into a DataFrame: spark.sql("SELECT * FROM parquet.`/data/users.parquet`"). The format name before the dot (for example parquet, orc, json, csv or text) selects the data source, and the path goes in backticks. The result is an ordinary DataFrame, so you can keep transforming it. This is convenient for exploration; production code usually reads with explicit options and a schema through spark.read, and then registers a view. A path is not a table: it creates no catalog entry, and the next session has to repeat the full path. When the files are partitioned in directories, the partition columns appear in the result and can be used in WHERE to prune directories. The same statement form works for directories of files, not only single files, and Spark still plans the query with Catalyst, so filters can be pushed to the file source, as the PushedFilters entry in explain output shows.

concepts.heading: Save Modes
concepts.body: A write checks what already exists at the target before it writes. df.write.mode(...) takes four values. error or errorifexists is the default and throws an exception if data already exists. append adds the new rows to the existing data. overwrite replaces the existing data. ignore silently does nothing if data exists, like CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. The documentation warns that save modes use no locking and are not atomic, and that with overwrite the existing data is deleted before the new data is written, so a failed job can leave the target empty or partial. For partitioned tables, the configuration page describes spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode: in the default static mode Spark deletes the matching partitions ahead of the overwrite, while dynamic mode overwrites only the partitions that receive data at runtime. It can also be passed as a write option. A frequent trap is rerunning a job that writes with the default mode: the second run fails because the path already exists. Output committers also vary, so a _SUCCESS marker file is not guaranteed on every store.

examPoints: CSV defaults: no header, no schema inference, all strings; JSON must be JSON Lines unless multiLine is set; writes produce a directory of part files.
JDBC reads use one partition unless partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions are all set; the bounds set the stride and do not filter.
Save modes: errorifexists (default), append, overwrite, ignore; they are neither atomic nor locked, and dynamic partition overwrite replaces only touched partitions.

quiz.q: A job reads a 10-million-row table with spark.read.format('jdbc') using only url, dbtable and credentials. What is the effect on parallelism?
choices: One partition and one connection are used until the partition column and its bounds are given
Spark splits the table into one partition per 128 MB automatically, using file size estimates
The read uses 200 partitions, the same as spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, because of the default shuffle setting
Spark opens one connection per executor core, so the load scales with the cluster size automatically
quiz.explain: Without partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions the JDBC source reads through one connection into one partition. The 128 MB setting applies to file sources and the shuffle setting to shuffles.

quiz.q: A daily job runs df.write.parquet('/out/sales') with no mode. On the second day the path already holds data. What happens?
choices: The new rows are appended to the existing files in the output folder
The existing data is replaced by the new data in the output folder
The write is skipped silently and the old data stays unchanged there
The job fails because the default mode is errorifexists
quiz.explain: The default save mode throws if data already exists at the target. Append, overwrite and ignore must be requested explicitly with mode().

days.recap: File readers have documented defaults (CSV strings, JSON Lines, Parquet default format) and writes produce directories of part files. JDBC needs four options together to read in parallel. SQL on files uses format.`path`. Save modes are errorifexists, append, overwrite and ignore, with no atomicity.

days.title: Persistent Tables with Sorting, Partitioning and Bucketing, and Temporary and Global Temp Views

concepts.heading: Saving to Persistent Tables
concepts.body: df.write.saveAsTable('sales') materializes the DataFrame and registers a pointer to the data in the metastore, so the table survives restarts of the program (as long as the same metastore is used) and spark.table('sales') or SQL can read it later. This is the difference from a temporary view, which stores only a query plan name. If you pass option('path', '/some/path') the table is external: dropping it removes the metadata but leaves the files. Without a path, Spark writes under the warehouse directory and the files are deleted when the table is dropped (a managed table). saveAsTable obeys the same save modes as other writes, so rerunning with the default mode fails when the table exists; overwrite replaces it and append adds rows. Partition information for external tables created with a path is not gathered by default, so MSCK REPAIR TABLE syncs it. The SQL equivalent is CREATE TABLE ... USING parquet AS SELECT .... In both forms the data source format decides the file layout.

concepts.heading: Partitioning, Bucketing and Sorting
concepts.body: Three layout options organize files for faster retrieval. partitionBy('country') writes one directory per distinct value; a filter on that column lets Spark skip whole directories. It works with save and saveAsTable but suits low-cardinality columns, because each distinct value creates a directory and high cardinality produces huge numbers of small files. bucketBy(n, 'col') hashes a column into a fixed number of buckets, so it suits columns with unbounded distinct values, and joins on the bucket column can avoid a shuffle when both tables are bucketed the same way on the join key, as the performance guide describes for bucket joins. sortBy('col') sorts rows inside each bucket. The documentation says bucketing and sorting are applicable only to persistent tables, so use saveAsTable rather than a plain file save. Partitioning and bucketing can be combined: df.write.partitionBy('c').bucketBy(42, 'k').sortBy('k').saveAsTable('t'). Remember that sortBy on the writer is not a global sort: it orders data only within each bucket file. For a total ordering use orderBy on the DataFrame.

concepts.heading: Temporary Views
concepts.body: A temporary view gives a DataFrame a SQL name without writing any data. df.createOrReplaceTempView('t') registers or replaces the name; createTempView('t') raises an error if the name already exists. The view is session-scoped: its lifetime is tied to the SparkSession that created it, it disappears when that session ends, and it is not visible in another session created with newSession(). It holds only the logical plan, so each query on it recomputes from the source unless the underlying DataFrame is cached. spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM t') returns a DataFrame, so SQL and DataFrame code interoperate freely, and you can build a chain of views for readability. A temporary view is not stored in any catalog schema or in the metastore, and no files are created. Views can be dropped with spark.catalog.dropTempView('t'). Registering a view also does not copy or cache data: if the source files change between two queries, the second query can see different rows.

concepts.heading: Global Temporary Views
concepts.body: A global temporary view is shared among all sessions of one Spark application and stays until the application terminates. df.createGlobalTempView('t') creates it in the system-preserved database global_temp, and you must use the qualified name, for example SELECT * FROM global_temp.t; the unqualified name t is not found. spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM global_temp.t') works because the view is cross-session. It does not outlive the application, so a new application or a restart no longer has it. For anything that must outlast the program, use saveAsTable instead. Choosing between the three: a session-scoped need such as breaking a long pipeline into readable SQL steps gets a temporary view; handing a DataFrame to another session in the same application gets a global temporary view; data that other applications must find gets a persistent table. The names also differ in how they fail: createTempView and createGlobalTempView raise an error when the name exists, and the createOrReplace form silently replaces it.

examPoints: saveAsTable registers a persistent table; with a path option it is external (files survive a drop), without it the files are deleted on drop.
partitionBy suits low-cardinality columns; bucketBy and sortBy work only with saveAsTable; sortBy orders within each bucket only.
Temporary view = one session; global temporary view = all sessions of the application, read as global_temp.name; neither survives the application.

quiz.q: A developer runs df.createGlobalTempView('orders') in one session. Which call works from another session of the same application?
choices: spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM global_temp.orders')
spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM default.orders LIMIT 5')
spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM global.orders LIMIT 5')
spark.newSession().sql('SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 5')
quiz.explain: Global temporary views live in the system database global_temp and must be referenced by the qualified name. An unqualified name only resolves session-scoped views.

quiz.q: Which write statement is valid for sorting rows within buckets and storing the result as a table?
choices: df.write.bucketBy(8, 'id').sortBy('ts').parquet('/out/t')
df.write.sortBy('ts').saveAsTable('t')
df.write.bucketBy(8, 'id').sortBy('ts').saveAsTable('t')
df.write.partitionBy('ts').sortBy('id').parquet('/out/t')
quiz.explain: Bucketing and sorting are documented only for persistent tables, so the write must end in saveAsTable, and sortBy orders rows inside buckets, so it is paired with bucketBy. Plain file saves are not the supported route.

days.recap: saveAsTable creates catalog tables; a path option makes them external. partitionBy, bucketBy and sortBy have different uses and bucketing needs saveAsTable. A temporary view lives in one session and a global temporary view lives in global_temp for the whole application; createTempView fails on an existing name.

days.title: Column and Row Manipulation, Deduplication and Validation

concepts.heading: Adding, Replacing, Renaming and Dropping Columns
concepts.body: Every DataFrame method returns a new DataFrame; the original never changes. `withColumn(name, expr)` adds a column or, when the name already exists, replaces that column, so `df.withColumn("price", F.col("price") * 2)` still has one `price` column. `withColumns({...})` (Spark 3.3) adds or replaces several columns from one dict. That matters in loops: each `withColumn` call introduces a projection internally, so a loop of hundreds of calls builds a big plan (the docs warn of performance problems and even a StackOverflowException), while one `withColumns` or `select` adds a single projection. `withColumnRenamed(old, new)` and the dict form `withColumnsRenamed` do nothing when the old name is missing, and `drop("a", "typo")` ignores names that are not in the schema, so neither call reports a typo. `select` with `alias`, or `selectExpr("price * qty AS total")`, projects only the columns you list, which is also how you reorder them. `filter` and `where` are aliases of each other and keep the rows for which the condition is true.

concepts.heading: Splitting Strings and Exploding Arrays
concepts.body: `F.split(str, pattern, limit=-1)` treats the pattern as a Java regular expression and returns an array. With `limit <= 0` the pattern is applied as often as possible; with `limit > 0` the array has at most that many entries and the last one holds everything after the last match, so `split("a-b-c-d", "-", 2)` returns `['a', 'b-c-d']`. Take one element with `getItem(i)`. `F.explode(col)` produces one row per array element (or per key and value of a map) and drops rows whose array is empty or NULL; `F.explode_outer` keeps them with a NULL value. `F.posexplode` adds a `pos` column next to the default `col`. A single `select` may hold only one generator such as `explode`, so to combine two arrays chain two `withColumn(..., F.explode(...))` steps, which yields every pairing of their elements. With ANSI mode on (the Spark 4 default), `element_at` raises an error for an index outside the array, while `try_element_at` returns NULL.

concepts.heading: Deduplication
concepts.body: `distinct()` removes rows that are identical in every column. `dropDuplicates(["id", "name"])` compares only the listed columns and keeps one row per combination; `drop_duplicates` is an alias. Every name in the subset must exist, otherwise Spark raises an `AnalysisException`, unlike `drop`. A batch `dropDuplicates` is planned as a grouped aggregate over the listed columns, so NULLs count as equal, as in GROUP BY and DISTINCT where all NULLs fall into one bucket, and two rows `(2, NULL)` collapse into one even though `NULL = NULL` is not true in a filter. Values compare by exact characters, so `Ana@x.com`, `ana@x.com` and `ana@x.com ` stay three emails until you normalize with `F.lower(F.trim("email"))`. The docs do not say which duplicate survives; when it matters, for example the latest row per key, use `row_number()` over a window partitioned by the key and ordered by the timestamp, then keep row number 1. To list repeated keys use `groupBy("id").count().filter("count > 1")`.

concepts.heading: Validation: NULLs, Fill Values and Safe Casts
concepts.body: Validation separates good rows from bad ones without losing either. `dropna(how="any"|"all", thresh=n, subset=[...])` removes rows with NULL or NaN values: `how="all"` drops a row only when every listed column is empty, and `thresh` keeps rows with at least that many non-null values. `fillna(value, subset)` replaces NULLs but ignores columns whose type does not match the value, so a string default leaves an int column alone; a dict gives one default per column. A filter keeps only rows where the predicate is true, so `between(0, 120)` and its negation both drop a NULL age; add `isNull()` to the invalid set. With ANSI mode on, `cast("int")` on the text `abc` raises an error instead of returning NULL. To validate text, use `Column.try_cast` (Spark 4.0; `try_cast(x AS INT)` in SQL), which returns NULL, and flag rows whose result is NULL although the input was not. `eqNullSafe` compares two columns and treats NULL as an ordinary value.

examPoints: withColumn with an existing name replaces that column; drop and withColumnRenamed ignore unknown names, but dropDuplicates with an unknown subset name fails.
explode drops empty and NULL arrays, explode_outer keeps them; only one generator is allowed per select; split with a positive limit keeps the rest in the last element.

distinct compares all columns, dropDuplicates(subset) only the listed ones, and both treat NULLs as equal; filters and their negations both lose NULL rows; under ANSI use try_cast to turn bad text into NULL.

quiz.q: A DataFrame `df` has the columns `id` and `tags` (array of strings) and the rows `(1, ['a','b'])`, `(2, [])` and `(3, NULL)`. How many rows does `df.select("id", F.explode_outer("tags").alias("tag")).count()` return?
choices: 3, because every id yields exactly one row no matter how many elements its array holds
4, because the empty and the NULL array each keep one row with a NULL tag
2, because only the rows whose array holds at least one element survive an explode of any kind
1, because explode_outer returns a single row that collects all elements of all arrays together
quiz.explain: explode_outer yields two rows for id 1 and one row each, with a NULL tag, for the empty array and the NULL array: 4 rows. Plain explode would return only the two rows of id 1.

quiz.q: `df` has the columns `id`, `name`, `ts` and the rows `(1,'a',10)`, `(1,'a',20)`, `(2,NULL,30)` and `(2,NULL,40)`. What do `df.distinct().count()` and `df.dropDuplicates(["id", "name"]).count()` return?
choices: 2 and 4, because the subset version keeps every row whose ts value differs
4 and 4, because rows containing a NULL in name are never treated as duplicates of each other
2 and 2, because distinct also ignores the ts column when it compares the rows
4 and 2, because the subset ignores ts and NULLs count as equal
quiz.explain: distinct compares all three columns, and no two rows are identical, so it returns 4. The subset id and name gives the groups (1,'a') and (2,NULL); NULLs count as equal in duplicate detection, so the result is 2.

days.recap: Column methods return new DataFrames: withColumn replaces by name, withColumns batches, drop and rename ignore missing names. split and explode reshape strings and arrays (explode_outer keeps empty ones). Deduplicate with distinct or dropDuplicates(subset), where NULLs are equal, and validate with dropna, fillna and try_cast, remembering that filters drop NULL rows.

days.title: Aggregations, Distinct Counts, Summary Statistics and Dates

concepts.heading: Counting, Averaging and Exact Distinct Counts
concepts.body: `df.count()` is an action that returns a Python int, while `df.groupBy("k").count()` is a transformation that returns a DataFrame with a `count` column. Inside `agg`, `F.count("*")` counts rows, and `F.count("x")` counts the rows where `x` is not NULL, because every aggregate function ignores NULL except `count(*)`. `F.count(expr)` counts non-NULL results of an expression, and a comparison such as `F.col("x") > 2` is false, not NULL, for a value of 1, so it is counted anyway; to count matches use `F.count(F.when(cond, 1))`. `F.mean` is an alias of `avg` and skips NULL, so 1, NULL, 3 give 2.0. `F.count_distinct(col)` skips NULL, so 1, 1, NULL, 2 give 2, while `distinct().count()` gives 3 because distinct keeps NULL as a value. With several columns it counts distinct combinations and skips a row if any listed column is NULL. With ANSI mode on, an integral overflow in `sum` raises an error; `try_sum` and `try_avg` return NULL instead.

concepts.heading: Approximate Counts, describe and summary
concepts.body: Exact distinct counts must shuffle every value, which is costly on billions of rows. `F.approx_count_distinct(col, rsd)` returns an estimate whose maximum relative standard deviation `rsd` defaults to 0.05; a smaller `rsd` tightens the error at a higher cost, and the docs note that below 0.01 `count_distinct` is the more efficient choice. `df.describe(*cols)` returns count, mean, stddev, min and max for numeric and string columns, all of them when no names are given. `df.summary(*statistics)` returns count, mean, stddev, min, the approximate quartiles `25%`, `50%`, `75%` and max by default, and you choose the rows by name: `df.summary("count", "50%", "max")` returns exactly those three, and any approximate percentile such as `90%` is accepted. For named results use `df.agg(F.mean("x").alias("avg_x"), F.max("x"))`, or `groupBy("store").agg(F.count_distinct("customer").alias("customers"))` for one row per group.

concepts.heading: Epoch Seconds, Strings and Dates under ANSI
concepts.body: A moment has three forms: epoch seconds (a bigint counted from 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC), a date or timestamp, and a formatted string. `from_unixtime(sec, fmt)` returns a string rendered in the session time zone `spark.sql.session.timeZone`, so `1767225600` becomes `2026-01-01` in UTC but `2025-12-31` in a zone behind UTC; set the zone explicitly. `unix_timestamp(str, fmt)` parses a string into epoch seconds, and `timestamp_seconds(n)` turns seconds into a timestamp. `to_date(str, fmt)` parses a string, where the format describes the input text. In ANSI mode a numeric cannot be cast to a date, so `col("ts").cast("date")` on a bigint is rejected, and `to_date` or `to_timestamp` on text that does not match raises an error; `try_to_date` (4.0) and `try_to_timestamp` (3.5) return NULL instead. Pattern letters are case sensitive: `yyyy`, `MM` month, `dd`, `HH` hour 0-23, `hh` hour 1-12, `mm` minute, `ss`.

concepts.heading: Date Components and Date Arithmetic
concepts.body: `year`, `month`, `quarter`, `dayofmonth`, `hour` and similar functions return integers, and `F.extract` or `date_part` take the field name. `dayofweek` counts from 1 for Sunday to 7 for Saturday, so 2024-03-10, a Sunday, gives 1. `date_format(col, "yyyy-MM")` returns a string, `trunc(date, "month")` returns a date and `date_trunc("month", ts)` returns a timestamp; note the swapped argument order of the two. `datediff(end, start)` returns the days between two dates with the later date first, so `datediff("ship_date", "order_date")` is positive for orders shipped after they were placed. `add_months(d, n)` moves by whole months and clips to the last day of a shorter month, so 2024-01-31 plus one month is 2024-02-29. `last_day(d)` returns the month end and `months_between` the fractional month distance. Date columns hold no time zone; timestamps display in the session time zone.

examPoints: count(*) counts rows, count(col) skips NULL, count_distinct skips NULL while distinct().count() keeps it; mean is avg and ignores NULL.
approx_count_distinct has rsd 0.05 by default; summary("count", "50%", "max") picks statistics, describe picks columns.

from_unixtime gives a string in the session time zone, unix_timestamp gives epoch seconds; under ANSI a bigint cannot be cast to date and bad text raises unless you use try_to_date or try_to_timestamp.

quiz.q: `df` has a column `x` with the values 4, NULL, 4 and 10. What does `df.agg(F.count("*"), F.count("x"), F.count_distinct("x"), F.mean("x")).first()` return?
choices: (4, 3, 2, 6.0), because count(*) keeps the NULL row and the mean skips it
(4, 4, 2, 4.5), because count(x) includes the NULL row and the mean divides by all four rows
(3, 3, 2, 6.0), because count(*) also skips the row whose x value is NULL
(4, 3, 3, 4.5), because count_distinct treats NULL as a third value and the mean divides by four
quiz.explain: count(*) counts 4 rows, count(x) skips the NULL and counts 3, count_distinct sees 4 and 10, which is 2, and the mean is (4 + 4 + 10) / 3 = 6.0 because aggregates ignore NULL.

quiz.q: A column `d` of type `date` holds 2024-01-31, a Wednesday. What does `df.select(F.datediff(F.lit("2024-03-01").cast("date"), F.col("d")).alias("n"), F.dayofweek("d").alias("w")).first()` return for `n` and `w`?
choices: n is -30 and w is 4, because the earlier date is the first argument of datediff
n is 29 and w is 3, because February is skipped and Wednesday is numbered from 1 for Monday
n is 30 and w is 4, because the end date comes first and Sunday is 1
n is 30 and w is 3, because Wednesday is the third weekday counted from Monday
quiz.explain: datediff(end, start) is positive here: 29 days to 2024-02-29 plus one more to 2024-03-01 is 30. dayofweek counts Sunday as 1, so Monday is 2, Tuesday 3 and Wednesday 4.

days.recap: Aggregates skip NULL except count(*); count_distinct is exact, approx_count_distinct trades accuracy through rsd, and describe or summary give quick statistics. Epoch seconds, timestamps and strings convert with from_unixtime, unix_timestamp, timestamp_seconds and to_date, and under ANSI mode bad text raises unless a try_ variant is used.

days.title: Joins, Set Operations and Broadcast Joins

concepts.heading: Join Basics: Keys, Types and Duplicates
concepts.body: `left.join(right, on, how)` defaults to `inner`. When `on` is a column name or a list of names, the names must exist on both sides, Spark performs an equi-join and keeps a single copy of each key column; when `on` is a Column expression such as `a.id == b.id`, both id columns stay in the result, and later references to `id` become ambiguous until you alias or drop one. The `how` values include `inner`, `left` / `left_outer`, `right`, `full` / `full_outer`, `cross`, `left_semi` and `left_anti`. Keys that are NULL never match, because `NULL = NULL` is not true; `eqNullSafe` lets NULLs pair up. Duplicate keys multiply rows: if two left rows and two right rows share a key, the result has four rows for it. Join on `["k1", "k2"]` to require all keys. Outer joins fill the missing side with NULLs, and a full outer join keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

concepts.heading: Semi, Anti and Cross Joins
concepts.body: `left_semi` is an existence filter: it returns the left rows that have at least one match, left columns only, each left row once however many matches exist, so it answers "customers with at least one order" without a later `dropDuplicates`. `left_anti` returns the left rows without a match; a left row with a NULL key has no match, so it appears in the result. Neither adds columns from the right side. A cross join pairs every left row with every right row: 1,000 rows and 50 rows give 50,000. `left.crossJoin(right)` states the intent. A `join` with no condition also produces the Cartesian product, because `spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled` is true by default since Spark 3.0, so a forgotten condition no longer fails loudly. Cartesian results grow multiplicatively, so an accidental one is a common cause of slow jobs and huge outputs.

concepts.heading: Union and Other Set Operations
concepts.body: `a.union(b)` appends the rows of `b` below `a` and keeps duplicates, so it behaves like SQL `UNION ALL`, and `unionAll` is the same method. Add `.distinct()` to get SQL `UNION`. Columns are matched by position, not by name, so two frames with the same columns in a different order are combined misaligned without any error; `a.unionByName(b)` matches by name, and `allowMissingColumns=True` (Spark 3.1) fills columns missing on one side with NULL. Other set operations follow SQL: `subtract` is `EXCEPT DISTINCT`, while `exceptAll` respects counts and also resolves columns by position; `intersect` removes duplicates and `intersectAll` keeps them. With `a` holding 1, 1, 2 and `b` holding 1, `a.subtract(b)` returns only 2, while `a.exceptAll(b)` returns 1 and 2, since one of the two 1 rows is cancelled.

concepts.heading: Broadcast Joins
concepts.body: A broadcast join copies the small side to every executor, so the large side is joined where it already is and is not shuffled. Spark plans it on its own when the estimated size of a side is at most `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default, -1 disables); above that you ask for it with `big.join(F.broadcast(small), "k")`, `small.hint("broadcast")` or, in SQL, `/*+ BROADCAST(r) */`, where `BROADCASTJOIN` and `MAPJOIN` are synonyms. When hints conflict, `BROADCAST` wins over `MERGE`, then `SHUFFLE_HASH`, then `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`. With an equality key the strategy is a broadcast hash join; without one (a range condition) it is a broadcast nested loop join. Collecting the small side takes time: `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` is 300 seconds. With Adaptive Query Execution on, a sort-merge join can also turn into a broadcast join at runtime when the real size turns out to be small. Do not confuse this with broadcast variables, which are the topic of day 10.

examPoints: Joining by name or list keeps one key column; NULL keys never match; left_semi returns left columns once per row, left_anti returns unmatched rows including NULL keys.
DataFrame union is UNION ALL and matches columns by position; use unionByName for names and distinct() for UNION; subtract removes duplicates, exceptAll respects counts.
Broadcast with F.broadcast, hint("broadcast") or a SQL hint; the 10 MB threshold and the 300 second timeout are the defaults; broadcast beats merge when hints conflict.

quiz.q: `a` has `id` values 1, 2, 2 and NULL. `b` has `id` values 2, NULL and 3. What does `a.join(b, "id", "left_semi").count()` return?
choices: 4, because a left_semi join returns every row of the left side
3, because the NULL row of the left side matches the NULL row of the right side
1, because each distinct matching key is returned once, however many left rows share it
2, because both left rows with id 2 match and NULL never matches NULL
quiz.explain: A semi join keeps each left row that has a match and never multiplies rows. Both rows with id 2 have a match in b, id 1 has none, and a NULL key matches nothing, so 2 rows come back.

quiz.q: `facts` is large. `dims` is the result of a filter, and the planner estimates 30 MB for it, so it plans a sort-merge join, although the developer knows only about 2 MB remain. The default threshold is unchanged. Which minimal change gets a broadcast join for this one join?
choices: Set spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to -1 for the whole session, so Spark always broadcasts
Use facts.join(dims.hint("broadcast"), "k"), which asks for dims as the broadcast side
Replace the join with facts.crossJoin(dims) and filter the matching keys afterwards
Call dims.repartition(200) first, so that every executor receives a part of dims
quiz.explain: A broadcast hint (or F.broadcast) requests the broadcast regardless of the size estimate. A threshold of -1 disables automatic broadcasting, a cross join is far more expensive, and repartitioning dims causes a shuffle rather than a broadcast.

days.recap: Pick the join type by the result you need: inner, outer, semi for existence, anti for absence, cross only on purpose. NULL keys never match and duplicate keys multiply rows. DataFrame union is UNION ALL by position. Broadcast joins avoid shuffling the large side, are planned under 10 MB or requested by a hint, and use a nested loop without an equality key.

days.title: Schemas on Read and Write, Sorting, Printing and Converting to Lists

concepts.heading: Reading with an Explicit Schema
concepts.body: `spark.read.schema("id INT, name STRING")` accepts a DDL string or a `StructType`. An explicit schema avoids the extra pass over the data that `inferSchema` needs for CSV, and it fixes the types: inference turns a zip such as `00742` into the number 742, so declare identifiers as `STRING`. For CSV, `header` defaults to false, so with a header line add `option("header", True)`; without it the header becomes a data row, and a value that cannot be parsed as `INT` turns into NULL. The schema is applied by position: with the default `enforceSchema=true` the header names are ignored, so the fields must be declared in the file's column order, and a mismatched order leaves wrong values in the wrong columns without any error. Set `enforceSchema` to false to have Spark check the header against the schema. Parquet and ORC files carry their own schema, so no inference is needed for them; Parquet columns are read as nullable.

concepts.heading: Malformed Records and JSON Layout
concepts.body: The `mode` option of the CSV and JSON readers controls what happens to a record that cannot be parsed. `PERMISSIVE` is the default: the bad fields become NULL, and if the schema contains a string column named `_corrupt_record` (or the name set with `columnNameOfCorruptRecord`) the raw text is stored there. `DROPMALFORMED` silently drops the bad rows, and `FAILFAST` raises an exception at the first one, which is the right choice when a nightly job must not hide bad input. Because reads are lazy, the failure appears when an action runs, not on the `read` line. JSON files are read as JSON Lines by default: every line is one complete object. A pretty-printed file, or one array spread over many lines, needs `option("multiLine", True)`; otherwise the DataFrame consists of a single `_corrupt_record` column. `samplingRatio` limits how many JSON objects or CSV rows schema inference reads.

concepts.heading: Schemas on Write and in the DataFrame
concepts.body: `df.schema` is a `StructType`, `df.dtypes` lists name and type pairs, `df.columns` the names, and `df.printSchema()` prints the tree, with `level` limiting the depth of nested fields. A list of Python tuples becomes `long` for an int, `string` for text and `array<string>` for a list, with `element` and `containsNull = true` shown for arrays, and inferred fields are nullable. Output formats differ: CSV stores neither names nor types, so a round trip without `header` on write and read gives `_c0`, `_c1` of type string, whereas Parquet and ORC preserve the schema. To change types before a write, cast the columns; under ANSI mode a `cast` or an insert into a table with a narrower type, for example a bigint that does not fit an int column, raises an overflow error, and `try_cast` returns NULL instead. Inserts into tables also follow `spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy`, which defaults to ANSI.

concepts.heading: Sorting, Iterating and Converting to Lists
concepts.body: `orderBy` and `sort` produce a global order, which needs a shuffle; `sortWithinPartitions` sorts each partition only, which is enough when every output file must be ordered. Mixed directions use `orderBy("dept", F.desc("salary"))`. Ascending order puts NULL first and descending puts NULL last by default; `asc_nulls_last()` and the related methods change that. `collect()` returns a list of `Row` objects on the driver, read as `rows[1]["v"]` or `rows[1].v`; `take(n)` and `head(n)` return a list, `limit(n)` returns a DataFrame. `toPandas()` and `collect()` load all rows into driver memory. `toLocalIterator()` streams the rows to the driver and needs memory for about the largest partition. `foreach` and `foreachPartition` run on the executors, so printing inside them does not show on the driver. `isEmpty()` is the cheap test for "any rows", better than `count() == 0`.

examPoints: A CSV schema is positional and header must be set explicitly; read identifiers as STRING; Parquet is self-describing and ignores inferSchema.
PERMISSIVE nulls bad fields, DROPMALFORMED drops rows, FAILFAST raises; pretty-printed JSON needs multiLine; failures surface at the action.
orderBy is a global sort, sortWithinPartitions is not; ascending puts NULL first; collect and toPandas need all data on the driver, toLocalIterator one partition at a time.

quiz.q: A CSV file has the header `id,qty` and the rows `1,5` and `2,oops`. The code `rows = spark.read.schema("id INT, qty INT").option("header", True).csv(path).collect()` runs with no `mode` option. What does `rows` contain?
choices: An exception, because the text oops cannot be converted to INT in any read mode
One row, `(1, 5)`, because malformed rows are dropped by default
Two rows, `(1, 5)` and `(2, None)`, because PERMISSIVE nulls the bad field
Three rows, because the header line is also kept as a data row when a schema is given
quiz.explain: The default mode is PERMISSIVE: the unparsable qty becomes NULL and the row stays. Dropping rows needs DROPMALFORMED, failing needs FAILFAST, and header is set, so the header line is not data.

quiz.q: `df` has a column `score` with the values 10, NULL and 30. What does `[r.score for r in df.orderBy("score").collect()]` return?
choices: [None, 10, 30], because ascending order places NULL first by default
[10, 30, None], because NULL is always the largest value in an ascending sort
[30, 10, None], because orderBy without a direction sorts from high to low
[10, None, 30], because orderBy keeps rows with a NULL key at their original position
quiz.explain: orderBy sorts ascending unless told otherwise, and ascending order puts NULL first. To move NULL to the end use asc_nulls_last().

days.recap: Read with an explicit schema, in file order for CSV, with header set and identifiers as strings; mode decides how bad records are handled, and JSON needs multiLine for pretty-printed files. printSchema, dtypes and schema describe the frame. Sort globally with orderBy, per partition with sortWithinPartitions, and bring data to the driver with collect, toLocalIterator or toPandas only when it fits.

days.title: UDFs, Stateful Operators, Broadcast Variables and Accumulators

concepts.heading: Python UDFs: Types, NULLs and Determinism
concepts.body: A UDF wraps a Python function so that it can run on column values: `F.udf(lambda s: ..., "int")`. The return type defaults to `StringType` when omitted, and `spark.udf.register("name", f, returnType)` makes it callable from SQL with the same default. The function receives `None` for a NULL, so `s.upper()` on a NULL fails the task with an exception in the worker; handle `None` inside the function. Spark does not guarantee short-circuiting for UDFs: an `AND` or `WHERE` null check may run after the UDF, so make the function null-aware and put the check inside it. A UDF is assumed deterministic, which allows the optimizer to merge or repeat calls; call `asNondeterministic()` for random or time-dependent logic. Built-in Spark functions are optimized for distributed processing, so prefer one from `pyspark.sql.functions` when it exists. Vectorized pandas UDFs process batches and are covered on day 16.

concepts.heading: Stateful Operators in Python
concepts.body: Stateful streaming code keeps data per key from one micro-batch to the next, for example a session record per user. `groupBy("user_id").applyInPandasWithState(func, outputStructType, stateStructType, outputMode, timeoutConf)` (Spark 3.4, Spark Connect from 3.5) calls `func(key, Iterator[pandas.DataFrame], state)` and expects an `Iterator[pandas.DataFrame]` back; `state` is a `GroupState` that the function reads and updates, and timeouts call it again with empty input. Since Spark 4.0 the docs encourage the new `transformWithState` operator over the legacy `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState`. Its Python form is `transformWithStateInPandas(statefulProcessor, outputStructType, outputMode, timeMode)`. The processor is a `StatefulProcessor` subclass: `init(self, handle)` declares state variables, for example `handle.getValueState("numViolations", schema)`, `handleInputRows(self, key, rows)` processes the rows of one key and yields pandas DataFrames, and `close()` cleans up. Plain object attributes are not durable state. Both operators need a full shuffle by the key.

concepts.heading: StateStores and RocksDB
concepts.body: The state of a stateful query lives in a StateStore on the executors and is saved to the checkpoint location after each batch, so a restarted query continues from its state. The default provider keeps all state in an in-memory map inside the executor JVM and backs it with files in a checkpoint file system. With millions of keys this produces large JVM garbage-collection pauses and uneven micro-batch times. Since Spark 3.2 a RocksDB provider keeps state in native memory and local disk instead; switch with `spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass", "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")` before the query starts. It serves streaming aggregations, `dropDuplicates`, stream-stream joins and the arbitrary stateful operators alike. Changelog checkpointing (`spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.changelogCheckpointing.enabled`, off by default) uploads small change logs instead of full snapshots at commit. Watermarks bound how long state is kept, so state without a watermark can grow without limit.

concepts.heading: Broadcast Variables and Accumulators
concepts.body: Spark has two shared-variable types besides ordinary closures. A broadcast variable, `bc = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(codes)`, caches a read-only value on each executor instead of shipping it with every task; tasks read `bc.value`, and the driver must not change the object afterwards. `bc.unpersist()` frees the executor copies and a later use re-broadcasts, while `bc.destroy()` is final. An accumulator, `acc = sc.accumulator(0)`, is the opposite direction: tasks can only add to it with an associative, commutative operation, and only the driver reads `acc.value`. Updates are lazy: nothing is added until an action runs the code. Inside an action such as `foreach` Spark applies each task's update once; inside a transformation, or a UDF in `withColumn`, updates can be applied again when tasks or stages are re-executed, so the total may be too high. On a cluster, a Python global changed inside a task changes only the executor's own copy, so the driver still sees `0` (in local mode it may work by accident, and Spark does not define the behavior). `SparkContext` is not available in Spark Connect.

examPoints: A Python UDF returns string unless a type is given, receives None for NULL, has no short-circuit guarantee so null checks belong inside it, and is deterministic unless marked asNondeterministic.
applyInPandasWithState takes (key, Iterator[pdf], state); transformWithStateInPandas declares state in init via the handle; large keyed state with GC pauses points to the RocksDB provider.
Broadcast variable: read-only, driver to tasks, unpersist or destroy. Accumulator: add-only, only the driver reads it, exactly once only for updates inside actions.

quiz.q: After the code `acc = sc.accumulator(0)`, then `sc.parallelize(range(4), 2).foreach(lambda x: acc.add(x))` runs on a cluster, what does `print(acc.value)` show on the driver?
choices: 0, because executor updates stay on the executors until collect() brings them back
6, because foreach is an action, so each task's update is applied once
12, because each of the two partitions adds the complete sum of the range
An error, because an accumulator cannot be updated from inside a lambda function
quiz.explain: foreach is an action, so the tasks add 0+1+2+3 = 6 and the driver reads the total. Accumulator updates need no collect call, and a lambda that calls add is allowed.

quiz.q: A UDF checks every value against a Python dict of 200,000 entries that it reads from a driver variable, and shipping the dict with each task is slow. Which change fits the Spark shared-variable model?
choices: Store the dict in an accumulator and let the UDF read acc.value for each row
Convert the dict to a global variable that each task updates for the executors
Create bc = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(d) and read bc.value inside the UDF
Call asNondeterministic() on the UDF, so Spark keeps the dict on each executor
quiz.explain: A broadcast variable caches a read-only value once per executor. Tasks cannot read an accumulator, a global changed in a task affects only that executor's copy, and determinism has no effect on how data is shipped.

days.recap: Python UDFs default to string, see None for NULL, give no short-circuit guarantee and are assumed deterministic. Stateful streaming code keeps per-key state in a StateStore: applyInPandasWithState and transformWithStateInPandas are the Python entry points, and RocksDB helps with millions of keys. Broadcast variables send read-only data to tasks, accumulators send add-only counts back to the driver.

days.title: Partitioning, Repartition, Coalesce and Skew

concepts.heading: Partitions Decide Parallelism
concepts.body: A stage runs one task per partition, and a task occupies one core, so the partition count caps how many cores can work at once. Too few partitions leave cores idle and make each task hold a large share of data, which risks spilling or out-of-memory errors. Too many tiny partitions make scheduling overhead larger than the work. The tuning guide recommends 2-3 tasks per core and notes that Spark handles tasks as short as 200 ms well, so having more partitions than cores is safe. Partition counts come from three places. File scans pack input into partitions of up to `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`, 128 MB by default. Wide operations such as `groupBy` and `join` create `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` partitions, 200 by default. And you set the number yourself with `repartition` or `coalesce`. Check `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` and the Stages tab before tuning: the symptom (idle cores, one slow task, spilling) tells you which direction to move.

concepts.heading: repartition Versus coalesce
concepts.body: `repartition(n)` always performs a full shuffle. It can raise or lower the partition count and balances sizes; with columns, `repartition(n, "id")` hash-partitions so equal keys land together. `repartitionByRange` (hint `REPARTITION_BY_RANGE`) partitions by ranges of the column values instead of hashing. `coalesce(n)` merges existing partitions as a narrow dependency without a shuffle: going from 1000 to 100 partitions, each new partition claims 10 old ones. It can only lower the count, and asking for more than the current number leaves the DataFrame unchanged, with no error. Use `coalesce` to cheaply shrink after a selective filter, and `repartition` to grow or balance. The PySpark docs warn about a drastic `coalesce(1)`: the whole upstream computation may then run on one node, because the merge propagates into earlier steps. `repartition(1)` adds a shuffle but keeps the upstream work parallel. In SQL the hints `COALESCE`, `REPARTITION` and `REPARTITION_BY_RANGE` match these APIs, while `REBALANCE` exists only as a hint and needs AQE.

concepts.heading: Recognizing and Handling Data Skew
concepts.body: Hash partitioning sends every row with the same key to one partition. If 70% of rows share `country = 'US'`, then `df.repartition("country")` creates one oversized partition and the stage waits for a single straggler. In the Spark UI the signature is a maximum task duration or shuffle read size many times the median. Remedies: partition by a column with many evenly used values, use `repartition(n)` without columns for round-robin balance, add a random salt to the key, or rely on AQE. For sort-merge joins, AQE splits a partition into evenly sized tasks when it is larger than `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor` (5) times the median and also larger than `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (256 MB). Both conditions must hold. Example: with a median of 100 MB, the factor limit is 500 MB, so a 400 MB partition is not skewed even though it passes 256 MB, while a 620 MB partition is. Skew handling is on by default when AQE is.

concepts.heading: Reducing Shuffle Volume
concepts.body: Shuffles write map output to disk and move it over the network, so they are among the most expensive steps. Reduce the data entering a wide operation instead of tuning around it. Filter rows and select only needed columns early, so less data is shuffled. Aggregate before a join when the join does not need row-level detail: partial aggregation happens per partition first, so joining 10 billion clicks reduced to one row per user and day shuffles far less than joining the raw clicks. Broadcast a small side so the large side is not shuffled at all. Avoid wide steps that add nothing, such as an extra `repartition`, `distinct` or a global `orderBy` that no consumer needs. With AQE on, small post-shuffle partitions are merged for you; with AQE off, lower `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` for small jobs, for example to 8 for 50 MB of data, because 200 tiny tasks cost more than they save. Raising the shuffle partition count helps when partitions are so big that they spill.

examPoints: `coalesce` is narrow, only reduces partitions and never errors when asked for more; `repartition` shuffles and can grow or balance; `coalesce(1)` can collapse upstream work into one task.
Skew in AQE needs both conditions: larger than factor (5) times the median and larger than 256 MB; one huge key shows as max task far above median in the Spark UI.
Cut shuffle volume by filtering early, aggregating before joins, broadcasting small sides and skipping needless repartition, distinct and global orderBy.

quiz.q: A DataFrame has 2,000 small partitions after a selective filter. The next steps are narrow, about 200 partitions are wanted, and equal sizes do not matter. Which call is cheapest?
choices: `df.repartition(200)`, because the full shuffle also balances the partition sizes for the steps that follow
`df.coalesce(200)`, which merges neighbouring partitions without a shuffle
`df.repartition(200, "id")`, which hash-partitions by key and is therefore cheaper than a round-robin shuffle of all rows
`df.sortWithinPartitions("id")`, because sorting inside each task lowers the number of partitions that exist
quiz.explain: Merging partitions as a narrow dependency avoids moving rows between executors. Both repartition forms shuffle everything, and a local sort never changes the partition count.

quiz.q: With AQE defaults (skew factor 5, threshold 256 MB), the shuffle for a sort-merge join has a median partition of 80 MB and other partitions of 300, 450 and 900 MB. Which are treated as skewed?
choices: All three, because each of them is larger than the 256 MB threshold on its own
Only 900 MB, because skew handling needs a partition above 10 times the median
None of them, because skew handling is limited to partitions that exceed 1 GB
450 MB and 900 MB, which exceed both 400 MB (5 x median) and 256 MB
quiz.explain: A partition must beat the factor limit of 5 x 80 = 400 MB and the 256 MB threshold. The 300 MB partition passes only the threshold; 450 and 900 MB pass both.

days.recap: Partitions equal tasks. coalesce merges without a shuffle and only shrinks; repartition shuffles and balances. Skew shows as one slow task; AQE splits partitions above 5 x median and 256 MB. Shrink shuffles by filtering, aggregating first and broadcasting.

days.title: Adaptive Query Execution, Logs and Memory Diagnosis

concepts.heading: What AQE Changes at Runtime
concepts.body: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) is a Spark SQL feature that uses runtime statistics to pick a more efficient plan, enabled by default since Spark 3.2.0 and controlled by the umbrella setting `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`. A normal plan is built before the query starts from estimates that are often wrong after filters, joins and user code. A shuffle ends a stage and writes map output, so Spark knows the true size of every shuffle partition when the stage finishes. AQE uses those numbers to re-optimize the stages that have not started yet. It does not cache stage output, add executors or rewrite the plan at analysis time, and it does not cancel work that already finished. Because it reacts at shuffle boundaries, a query without a shuffle gains nothing: the scan's partition count comes from `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (128 MB by default) and the file layout, so fix a bad scan with `repartition(n)` after reading or by writing better-sized files.

concepts.heading: Coalescing, Join Switching and Skew Splitting
concepts.body: AQE applies three main optimizations. Coalescing merges contiguous small post-shuffle partitions when `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled` is true (the default). It starts from `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.initialPartitionNum`, or `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` if that is unset, and can only reduce the count. With `parallelismFirst` true (the default) it ignores the 64 MB advisory size and respects only the 1 MB minimum, so a 30 MB aggregation can end in far fewer tasks than 200. Join switching turns a sort-merge join into a broadcast hash join when a side's runtime size is under `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, which defaults to `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`. Setting that static value to `-1` therefore also disables the runtime switch unless the adaptive one is set separately. Skew splitting breaks oversized sort-merge join partitions into even tasks. The docs advise a large initial partition number and letting Spark pick the final one, so one setting handles a 1 GB day and a 2 TB day.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Out-of-Memory Failures
concepts.body: First find where memory ran out. If `collect()` aborts with a message about `spark.driver.maxResultSize` (default 1g), the serialized results exceeded the limit that protects the driver. Aggregate on the cluster, for example `groupBy("country").count()`, and collect only the small result. If tasks fail with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` during a join, each reduce task builds a hash table for its share, so the simplest fix is more parallelism: raise `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` or `repartition(n)` first so every task's input is smaller. If a cluster manager kills executors for exceeding the container limit and the logs show no `OutOfMemoryError`, raise `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, the non-heap memory that covers Python workers and native libraries; its default is executor memory times 0.10 (0.40 for non-JVM jobs on Kubernetes) with a 384 MiB floor, supported on YARN and Kubernetes. A task payload warning means a large driver-side object travels inside every task; send it once with a broadcast variable. The tuning guide treats tasks above about 20 KiB as worth optimizing.

concepts.heading: Reading Logs, the Spark UI and GC Evidence
concepts.body: Every application serves the Spark UI on port 4040 of the driver, with stages and tasks, storage, environment and executors. By default it vanishes when the application ends. To inspect past runs, set `spark.eventLog.enabled` to true with a shared `spark.eventLog.dir`, and point a Spark History Server at that directory with `spark.history.fs.logDirectory`; keeping the driver alive with a sleep loop is not the answer. Use the tabs to match symptoms: few tasks in the Stages tab with idle cores in the Executors tab is underutilization, such as a `coalesce(4)` placed before a slow UDF on a 32-core cluster, fixed by repartitioning to a multiple of the cores before the UDF. For garbage collection, add `-verbose:gc -XX:+PrintGCDetails` through `spark.executor.extraJavaOptions`; the output lands in the workers' stdout files, not on the driver. A full GC invoked several times before a task finishes means there is not enough memory for task execution. An old generation close to full means lowering `spark.memory.fraction` to cache less.

examPoints: AQE re-plans from shuffle-stage statistics: coalesces small partitions, switches sort-merge to broadcast hash join, splits skewed partitions; a plan without a shuffle gets no benefit.

Match the OOM to the fix: collect and maxResultSize means aggregate first; heap OOM in reduce tasks means more partitions; killed containers without OutOfMemoryError means memoryOverhead; large task payload means broadcast.
Past runs need `spark.eventLog.enabled` plus a History Server; GC logs sit on executors, and several full GCs per task mean too little execution memory.

quiz.q: A join is planned as sort-merge because Spark overestimates the size of one input. After the first shuffle stage a runtime statistic shows this side is only 5 MB. AQE is on with defaults. What can AQE do?
choices: Switch the remaining join to a broadcast hash join, since the runtime size is under the adaptive threshold
Keep the sort-merge join, because Spark fixes the join strategy before the first stage and never revises it while the query runs
Cancel the finished shuffle stage and restart the whole query so the small side is broadcast from the beginning of the plan
Replace the join with a cross join, because small inputs can be matched against every row of the large side
quiz.explain: AQE re-optimizes the stages that have not started, using real sizes from the shuffle. It does not restart finished work, and it never turns an equi-join into a cross join.

quiz.q: PySpark executors on Kubernetes are killed mid-stage for exceeding their pod memory limit. The executor logs show no OutOfMemoryError, and the job uses Python UDFs and native libraries. Which setting should be raised first?
choices: `spark.driver.maxResultSize`, which caps the serialized task results the driver accepts for one action
`spark.eventLog.compress`, which decides whether the event log is compressed before it reaches storage
`spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, the non-heap memory per executor
`spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`, which sets the target size of shuffle partitions after coalescing
quiz.explain: The container limit is heap plus non-heap memory. Python workers and native libraries use the non-heap part, and the manager kills the process before the JVM can throw an error.

days.recap: AQE uses real shuffle statistics to coalesce, switch joins and split skew, but only at shuffle boundaries. Pick the OOM fix by location: driver result, task heap, container overhead, task size. Keep event logs and a History Server for past runs.

days.title: Structured Streaming Engine, Output Modes and Sinks

concepts.heading: The Programming Model
concepts.body: Structured Streaming treats a live stream as a table that keeps growing. You write the same DataFrame or SQL operations as for a batch query, and Spark runs them incrementally on the new rows, updating a result table. Many other engines make you maintain running aggregates and reason about delivery guarantees yourself; here Spark owns that work. Because a stream never ends, actions that return a result immediately do not work: `count()` raises an `AnalysisException`, so use `groupBy().count()`, which is a streaming DataFrame holding a running count. `show()` is replaced by the console sink, and `foreach()` by `writeStream.foreach`. `limit`, `take` and `distinct` are unsupported, and sorting is allowed only after an aggregation in complete mode. File-based sources require an explicit schema by default, so `spark.readStream.format("json").load(path)` fails until you pass `.schema(...)`, or set `spark.sql.streaming.schemaInference` to true for ad-hoc work. The schema stays consistent across restarts.

concepts.heading: Micro-Batches and Triggers
concepts.body: By default a query runs as a series of small batch jobs, a micro-batch engine with latencies down to about 100 ms and exactly-once guarantees.
